lessons.title: Computational Thinking
lessons.description: How abstraction, decomposition and algorithmic thinking turn big problems into solvable steps.
lessons.content_html:
Every day, computers help us solve problems that would take a person hours — finding the quickest route home, sorting thousands of songs, or checking millions of records in seconds. But a computer cannot work anything out for itself. Before a problem can be handed to a machine, a human has to work out exactly how it will be solved. Computational thinking is the name we give to this way of tackling problems, and it is the foundation of everything a programmer does.

Computational thinking is built on three main principles: abstraction, decomposition and algorithmic thinking. Used together, they turn a large, messy, real-world problem into something precise enough for a computer to handle. This lesson looks at each principle in turn and then shows how they work together.

Abstraction

Abstraction means removing or hiding the details that do not matter, so that you can focus on the information that does. Almost every problem contains detail that is not needed to solve it. Filtering that detail out makes the problem simpler and much easier to work with.

A classic example is the London Underground map designed by Harry Beck. A real, geographically accurate map of the tunnels would be cluttered and confusing. Beck’s design throws away the true distances and the exact positions of the stations, and keeps only what a passenger actually needs: the order of the stations, which line each one is on, and where the lines connect. As geography the map is ‘wrong’, yet it is far more useful for planning a journey — that is abstraction at work.

Abstraction is everywhere in computing. When you drive a car, the steering wheel and pedals let you control the vehicle without knowing how the engine works — the mechanical detail is hidden from you. In a program, giving a value a sensible name such as score or playerName is abstraction too: the name lets you think about what the data means while hiding the binary and memory details underneath.

Key Fact

Abstraction removes unnecessary detail while keeping the key details needed to solve the problem. It does not mean throwing everything away — it means deciding what matters and what can be ignored.

Decomposition

Decomposition means breaking a big, complicated problem into smaller parts. Each smaller part is called a sub-problem, and each one can be solved on its own. Trying to solve one huge problem all at once is hard; solving a series of small, clear problems is far more manageable.

Imagine you are asked to write a quiz app. As one giant task it feels overwhelming, and it is difficult to even know where to begin. Once it is decomposed, it becomes a list of smaller jobs that you can tackle one at a time.

A quiz app might break down into these sub-problems:

  • store the questions along with their correct answers
  • display one question at a time to the player
  • collect the player’s answer and check whether it is correct
  • keep a running score and show the final result at the end

Each sub-problem is small enough to solve, test and fix on its own. Decomposition also lets a team split the work between them, and a solved sub-problem — such as keeping score — can often be reused in a completely different program.

Algorithmic thinking

Algorithmic thinking is working out the exact steps needed to solve a problem, in the right order. The result of this thinking is an algorithm — a clear set of instructions that reliably leads to the correct result.

You already use algorithms in everyday life. A recipe is an algorithm: a list of steps, in order, that turns raw ingredients into a finished meal. Directions to a friend’s house are an algorithm too. If the steps are muddled, or a step is missing, you end up with the wrong result.

Algorithmic thinking means being precise. A computer follows instructions exactly, so a vague step like ‘check the answers’ is not enough. You have to spell each step out: get the player’s answer, compare it with the correct answer, and if they match, add one to the score. Spotting repeated patterns — such as doing that same check for every question — is an important part of thinking algorithmically.

Key Fact

An algorithm must have its steps in the correct order and each step must be precise. A computer does exactly what it is told, so an unclear or out-of-order step will produce the wrong output.

Putting the three together

The three principles are at their most powerful when combined. Suppose you want a program that finds the highest score in a class. Decomposition breaks the task into reading the scores, comparing them, and showing the result. Abstraction lets you ignore who sat where or when the test was taken — only the scores themselves matter. Algorithmic thinking gives you the ordered steps: treat the first score as the highest so far, then check each remaining score and replace the highest whenever you find a bigger one.

Watch out for these common misunderstandings:

  • Abstraction is not the same as decomposition — abstraction removes detail, while decomposition breaks a problem into parts.
  • An algorithm is the finished set of steps; algorithmic thinking is the process of working those steps out.
  • Abstraction keeps the important detail — it does not simply mean ‘making things shorter’.

Master these three principles and you have the core toolkit of a computer scientist — a dependable way to take any problem, however large, and shape it into something a computer can solve.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Read the command word carefully. ‘State’ or ‘identify’ wants a short, direct answer, while ‘describe’ and ‘explain’ want you to develop the point — and ‘explain’ usually means giving a reason or a consequence. A very common error is to define a term when the question asks you to apply it. If a question describes a particular program or system, use that context in your answer instead of writing a general definition.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Abstraction removes unnecessary detail so you can focus on the information that matters.
  • Decomposition breaks a large problem into smaller sub-problems that are easier to solve, test and share.
  • Algorithmic thinking works out the precise, ordered steps that form an algorithm to solve the problem.

lessons.title: Designing Algorithms (Pseudocode & Flowcharts)
lessons.description: Turn a problem into a plan using structure diagrams, pseudocode, flowcharts and trace tables.
lessons.content_html:
Before a programmer writes any code, they design an algorithm. An algorithm is a precise set of step-by-step instructions for solving a problem or completing a task. Planning the algorithm first — on paper or on screen — means you can spot mistakes in the logic before you spend time typing real program code. This lesson looks at four tools for designing algorithms: working out the inputs and outputs, drawing structure diagrams, and writing the steps as pseudocode or as a flowchart.

Inputs, processes and outputs

A good first step is to ask three questions: what information does the program need, what must it do with that information, and what should it produce? These are the inputs, the processes and the outputs. Take a program that works out the area of a rectangle. The inputs are the length and the width. The process is multiplying the length by the width. The output is the area, shown on the screen. Splitting a problem this way makes the design far clearer before you start coding.

Key Fact

Every program can be described by its inputs (the data going in), its processes (the steps that transform the data) and its outputs (the results that come out). Working these out first is the foundation of a good algorithm.

Breaking a problem down

Large problems are much easier to solve when they are split into smaller parts. This is called decomposition. A structure diagram shows this breakdown as a hierarchy: the whole problem sits in a box at the top, and the sub-tasks branch out beneath it, with the smallest jobs at the bottom. Reading from top to bottom takes you from the general goal down to the specific tasks the program must carry out.

Imagine building a quiz game. At the top is the whole task, ‘Run quiz game’. This breaks into three sub-tasks: ‘Ask questions’, ‘Keep score’ and ‘Show result’. ‘Ask questions’ then breaks down further into ‘Display question’, ‘Get answer’ and ‘Check answer’. Each of these small boxes is now simple enough to turn straight into code.

Run quiz game
    Ask questions
        Display question
        Get answer
        Check answer
    Keep score
    Show result

Writing pseudocode

Pseudocode is a way of writing an algorithm using short, code-like English. It is not a real programming language, so it does not have to follow exact syntax rules — but it does use common keywords so the logic is clear and could be turned into real code in any language. Pseudocode is quick to write and easy to read, which makes it ideal for planning.

score = input("Enter your score")
score = int(score)
if score >= 70 then
    print("Grade: Pass with merit")
elseif score >= 50 then
    print("Grade: Pass")
else
    print("Grade: Try again")
endif

This short algorithm shows the three building blocks that every algorithm is made from. Sequence means the steps run one after another, in order. Selection means the program chooses between different paths using a condition, such as the if … then … else above. Iteration means repeating a set of steps, using loops such as for or while.

Assignment gives a value to a variable, written as total = 0. Input and output are usually written as input and print. Selection uses if, then, elseif, else and endif. Iteration uses a count-controlled loop, for i = 1 to 10 … next i, or a condition-controlled loop, while … endwhile. A variable is a named store that holds a value which can change while the program runs.

Key Fact

Algorithms are built from just three constructs: sequence (steps in order), selection (choosing a path with a condition) and iteration (repeating steps in a loop). Every program, however complex, is made from these three.

Drawing flowcharts

A flowchart is a diagram that shows an algorithm as a series of boxes joined by arrows. The shape of each box tells you what kind of step it is, and the arrows show the order the steps run in. Flowcharts are especially good at showing decisions and loops clearly.

Each flowchart is built from a standard set of symbols:

  • Terminal — a rounded box that marks the start or the stop of the algorithm.
  • Process — a rectangle for an action or a calculation, such as adding one to a score.
  • Input/output — a parallelogram (a slanted box) for data going in or results coming out.
  • Decision — a diamond holding a yes/no or true/false question, with a branch leaving each answer.
  • Sub program — a rectangle with double side lines that calls a separate, named routine.
  • Flow line — an arrow that connects the symbols and shows the direction of flow.

The real power of a flowchart comes from the decision symbol. A loop is drawn by sending one branch of a decision back to an earlier point, so the steps repeat until the condition is met. Following the arrows from the start terminal to the stop terminal traces the whole algorithm.

A login check starts at a terminal marked ‘Start’. An input/output symbol asks the user to enter a password. A decision symbol then asks ‘Is the password correct?’. If the answer is yes, a process grants access and the flow reaches the stop terminal. If the answer is no, the flow line loops back to the input symbol so the user can try again.

Checking an algorithm with a trace table

Once an algorithm is designed, you can check it works using a trace table. This is a grid with a column for each variable and each output. You work through the algorithm by hand, one step at a time, writing down how the values change. Trace tables are the best way to find logic errors, especially inside loops, because they show exactly what the program would do.

Suppose a loop starts with total = 0 and adds the numbers 3, then 5, then 2. A trace table records the value of total after each pass through the loop: it starts at 0, becomes 3, then 8, then 10. If the final total is not what you expected, the table shows you the exact step where the logic went wrong.

Stepnumbertotal
Start—0
Pass 133
Pass 258
Pass 3210

Pseudocode or flowchart?

Both tools describe the same algorithm, so which you choose is often up to you. Pseudocode is fast to write and translates easily into real code, so programmers often prefer it for longer designs. Flowcharts are more visual and make branching and loops easy to see at a glance, which helps when explaining an idea to someone else. A skilled designer can move comfortably between the two.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When a question asks you to ‘complete’ or ‘refine’ an algorithm, read the existing lines carefully first — your answer must fit the style already used. If you are asked to ‘write’ an algorithm you may use pseudocode or a flowchart unless the question names one, but keep your steps in a clear order and label your inputs and outputs. For a ‘trace table’ question, fill in one row per step and never skip a loop pass, because the marks are given for showing every change to the values.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Design an algorithm before coding: identify the inputs, processes and outputs, then break the problem down with a structure diagram.
  • Pseudocode and flowcharts both describe an algorithm using the three constructs of sequence, selection and iteration.
  • A trace table checks an algorithm by recording how each variable changes, step by step, which reveals logic errors.

lessons.title: Searching Algorithms
lessons.description: Linear and binary search: how each one works, how fast they are, and when to use them.
lessons.content_html:
A searching algorithm is a set of clear steps for finding a particular piece of data inside a collection — like looking up a name in a contacts list or a product in an online shop. Two standard searching methods appear again and again in computing: the linear search and the binary search. Both reach the same goal — locating an item — but they go about it in very different ways, and each one suits different situations.

Linear search

A linear search is the most straightforward method. It starts at the very first item in the list and compares it with the target — the value being searched for. If the two match, the search is over and the position is reported. If they do not match, the algorithm simply moves on to the next item and compares again.

This checking continues, one item at a time, until either the target is found or the end of the list is reached. If the end is reached without a match, the algorithm reports that the item is not in the list. Because it never assumes anything about the order of the data, a linear search works on any list at all.

Key Fact

A linear search has no prerequisites: it works whether the data is sorted or not. That makes it flexible, but it can be slow because it may have to check every single item.

How efficient is it? Each time the algorithm checks one item against the target, that counts as one comparison. In the best case the target is the first item, so only one comparison is needed. In the worst case the target is the last item — or missing entirely — and the algorithm must make as many comparisons as there are items in the list.

Imagine searching the unsorted list 34, 7, 19, 45, 2, 88 for the value 45. The algorithm checks 34 (no match), then 7 (no match), then 19 (no match), then 45 — a match, found at the fourth position after four comparisons. If instead we searched for 15, the algorithm would check all six items, reach the end without a match, and report that 15 is not in the list. Notice that the list did not need to be in order for this to work.

Binary search

A binary search is much faster, but it comes with one strict condition: the list must already be sorted, meaning the items are arranged in order such as numbers from smallest to largest. When the data is sorted, a binary search can rule out huge chunks of the list at once instead of plodding through it item by item.

It works by finding the middle item of the list and comparing it with the target. If they match, the search is finished. If the target is smaller than the middle item, the algorithm throws away the middle item and the entire upper half, then repeats on the lower half. If the target is larger, it throws away the lower half and repeats on the upper half. Each pass finds a new middle and discards half of what remains, until the item is found or nothing is left to check.

Key Fact

A binary search only works on sorted data, and it halves the number of items still to check with every comparison. That is why it is so fast on large lists.

Suppose the sorted list is 2, 5, 8, 12, 16, 23, 38, 45, 56, 72, 91 and we are looking for 45. First the algorithm checks the middle value, 23. Because 45 is larger than 23, the whole lower half is discarded and only 38, 45, 56, 72, 91 remain. The new middle value is 56; 45 is smaller, so 56 and everything above it is discarded, leaving 38 and 45. The middle of these two rounds down to 38; 45 is larger, so only 45 is left, and the next check finds it. The target was found in just four comparisons, whereas a linear search would have taken eight.

Comparing the two searches

The big difference is speed on large lists. A linear search may have to look at every item, so searching a list of one thousand items could take up to one thousand comparisons. A binary search halves the remaining items with every check, so the same list of one thousand items needs at most about ten comparisons. It scales remarkably well: doubling the size of the list adds only one extra comparison to a binary search.

So why not always use a binary search? Because it only works on a sorted list. If the data is not in order, it must be sorted first, and sorting takes time and effort. A linear search has no such requirement — it happily works on data in any order and is very simple to write. For short lists the speed difference is tiny, so the extra work of keeping data sorted may not be worth it.

If the data set is small, or if it changes often and is rarely kept in order, a linear search is usually the sensible choice because it is simple and needs no preparation. If the data is large and already sorted — or will be searched many times — a binary search is far more efficient. Remember that sorting a list takes time too, so a binary search pays off most when the same sorted list is searched again and again.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Questions often give you a list and ask you to apply a search to it, so practise tracing each step and counting the comparisons. If a question asks you to identify an algorithm from its steps, the giveaway for a binary search is that it checks a middle value and discards half of the data — and remember it can only be used on a sorted list. Watch the command words: ‘describe’ wants the ordered steps, while ‘compare’ wants clear differences between the two methods.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • A linear search checks each item in turn and works on data in any order, but it can be slow on long lists because it may check every item.
  • A binary search is much faster because it halves the search area each pass, but the list must be sorted first.
  • Choose a linear search for small or unsorted data, and a binary search for large sorted lists that are searched often.

lessons.title: Sorting Algorithms
lessons.description: How bubble, insertion and merge sort put a list in order, and which one to pick.
lessons.content_html:
A list is far easier to work with when its items are in order. An ordered list is quicker to scan by eye, quicker to search with a computer, and some fast search methods will only work at all once the data has been arranged from smallest to largest. Putting items into order — ascending numbers, or names into alphabetical order — is the job of a sorting method.

A sorting algorithm takes an unordered list and rearranges it into the required order. There is no single ‘best’ sorting algorithm; each one trades speed, memory use and simplicity against the others. This lesson looks at three of them — bubble sort, insertion sort and merge sort — and at how to judge which is the better choice for a job.

Bubble sort

Bubble sort works by comparing pairs of neighbouring items and swapping them when they are in the wrong order. A swap simply exchanges the two values. Starting from the front, the algorithm compares the first and second items, then the second and third, and so on to the end of the list.

Each complete run through the list is called a pass. During the first pass the largest value keeps being swapped rightwards until it reaches the end — it ‘bubbles’ to the top. Bubble sort keeps making passes, each one settling the next-largest value into place, until it completes a whole pass without making a single swap. When that happens the list is known to be in order.

Key Fact

Bubble sort only ever compares adjacent items. After each full pass, the largest remaining value is guaranteed to be in its correct place at the end of the list.

Sort the list 5, 1, 4, 2 into ascending order. Pass 1: compare 5 and 1, they are in the wrong order so swap → 1, 5, 4, 2. Compare 5 and 4, swap → 1, 4, 5, 2. Compare 5 and 2, swap → 1, 4, 2, 5. The largest value, 5, has now bubbled to the end. Pass 2: compare 1 and 4, no swap; compare 4 and 2, swap → 1, 2, 4, 5. A final pass makes no swaps at all, so the algorithm stops — the list is sorted.

Insertion sort

Insertion sort builds a sorted section at the start of the list, one item at a time. The very first item is treated as a sorted list of one. The algorithm then takes the next unsorted item and inserts it into its correct position within the already-sorted section, shifting any larger items one place to the right to make room.

This is much like sorting a hand of playing cards: you pick up each new card and slide it into the right spot among the cards you already hold. Because insertion sort moves items by shifting them along rather than repeatedly swapping across the whole list, it is often very quick when a list is already nearly in order — each new item usually needs to move only a short distance.

Sort the list 3, 7, 4, 1. The sorted section starts as just [3]. Take 7: it is larger than 3, so it stays where it is → [3, 7]. Take 4: it is smaller than 7, so shift 7 right; it is larger than 3, so insert 4 between them → [3, 4, 7]. Take 1: it is smaller than every sorted item, so shift 7, 4 and 3 each one place right and place 1 at the front → [1, 3, 4, 7]. The list is now sorted.

Merge sort

Merge sort uses a strategy called divide and conquer. It repeatedly splits the list in half, and splits the halves again, until every sub-list holds just a single item. A list of one item cannot be out of order, so each of these tiny lists is already sorted.

The clever part is the merging. Two sorted sub-lists are combined by repeatedly comparing their front items and taking the smaller one, until all the values have been copied into a single, larger sorted list. This merging is repeated, joining pairs of sub-lists into ever-longer sorted lists, until one fully sorted list remains.

Key Fact

Merge sort first splits the list down to single items, then merges pairs back together in order. A sub-list of one item is treated as already sorted because a single value cannot be out of order.

Sort the list 6, 2, 7, 1. Split it into [6, 2] and [7, 1], then split again into [6], [2], [7] and [1]. Now merge: [6] and [2] combine to [2, 6]; [7] and [1] combine to [1, 7]. Finally merge [2, 6] with [1, 7]: compare 2 and 1, take 1; compare 2 and 7, take 2; compare 6 and 7, take 6; then take the last value, 7. The result is [1, 2, 6, 7].

Comparing the algorithms

Bubble sort and insertion sort are simple to understand and easy to write. They also work in place, meaning they need very little extra memory. Their weakness is speed: as a list grows, the number of comparisons they must make rises steeply, so they become slow on large amounts of data.

Merge sort copes far better with large lists — the amount of work it does grows much more gently as the list gets longer. The trade-off is that it needs extra memory to hold all the sub-lists while they are being merged, and it is more complicated to write than the other two.

As a rule of thumb, the simple sorts are perfectly good for short lists, while merge sort is usually the better choice for large ones. Of the three, bubble sort generally does the most comparing and swapping, so in practice it tends to be the slowest.

Key Fact

Merge sort is much faster than bubble sort on large lists, but it uses more memory because it must store the sub-lists while merging them.

Watch the command word closely: ‘describe’ wants the steps of one algorithm, while ‘compare’ wants clear differences between algorithms, usually covering both how they work and how efficient they are. A common slip is forgetting that bubble sort settles the largest value at the end after the first pass, not the smallest.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Bubble sort compares adjacent items and swaps them, making repeated passes until a pass has no swaps; the largest value settles at the end each pass.
  • Insertion sort grows a sorted section at the front, shifting larger items right to slot each new item into place — fast on nearly-sorted lists.
  • Merge sort splits the list into single items then merges them back in order; it is faster on large lists but uses more memory than the simple sorts.

lessons.title: Programming Fundamentals
lessons.description: Variables, constants, operators and the three constructs that control every program.
lessons.content_html:
Every app, game and website you use is built from a small number of simple ideas. Master these building blocks and you can read and write code in almost any language. This lesson covers four of them: storing information in variables and constants, changing that information with operators, and controlling the order in which instructions run.

Storing data: variables and constants

A variable is like a labelled box in the computer’s memory. The label is its name, and inside the box is a value your program can read or change at any time. A game might use a variable called score that starts at zero and grows as the player collects points. Because the value can change while the program is running, we say a variable is mutable.

A constant is also a named value, but it is set once and never changes while the program runs. Good examples are a rate of VAT, the value of pi, or the maximum number of lives in a game. Using a constant makes a program easier to read and safer, because an important value cannot be altered by mistake.

Key Fact

The key difference is change. A variable’s value can change while the program is running; a constant’s value is fixed and stays the same throughout.

Assignment, input and output

To put a value into a variable we use assignment, written with a single equals sign. The computer works out the right-hand side first, then stores the result in the variable named on the left. This is why score = score + 10 makes sense: it means ‘take the current score, add ten, and store the answer back in score’.

score = 0
name = input("Enter your name: ")
score = score + 10
print(name)
print(score)

Most programs also need to talk to the user. An input command reads something typed by the user so you can store it in a variable, while an output command (often written as print) displays a value on screen. Together, input, assignment and output let a program take data in, work on it, and show a result.

In everyday maths, x = x + 1 is impossible — a number cannot equal itself plus one. In programming the equals sign is not a question about whether two things are the same; it is an instruction to store a value. x = x + 1 tells the computer to take the current value of x, add one, and put the answer back. To test whether two values are the same, programmers use the double equals operator == instead.

Operators

An operator is a symbol or keyword that acts on data. The arithmetic operators do the maths you already know — addition with +, subtraction with -, multiplication with * and division with / — plus three that are especially useful in programming.

  • Normal division uses / and can give a decimal, so seventeen divided by five is 3.4.
  • DIV gives the whole-number quotient, meaning how many whole times one number goes into another, so 17 DIV 5 is 3.
  • MOD gives the remainder, or modulo, that is left over, so 17 MOD 5 is 2.
  • ^ raises a number to a power, known as exponentiation, so 3 ^ 2 is 9.
Key Fact

DIV and MOD work as a pair. DIV gives the whole number of times a division fits, and MOD gives what is left over. So 23 DIV 4 is 5, and 23 MOD 4 is 3.

Comparison operators ask a true-or-false question about two values. They are: equal to ==, not equal to !=, less than <, less than or equal to <=, greater than >, and greater than or equal to >=. Notice that testing for equality uses two equals signs, which keeps it clearly separate from assignment.

Boolean operators let you combine these true-or-false results. AND is true only when both conditions are true, OR is true when at least one condition is true, and NOT reverses a result, turning true into false and false into true.

Imagine a website that lets someone register only if they are aged 13 or over and have ticked the terms box. In code this becomes age >= 13 AND agreed == true. Both parts must be true for the whole condition to be true. If you swapped AND for OR, a person could register by doing just one of the two things — which is exactly why choosing the right Boolean operator matters.

The three programming constructs

Every program controls the order its instructions run using just three building blocks, called constructs. Almost all software is these three, combined and nested inside one another.

Sequence simply means the computer carries out instructions one after another, from top to bottom, in the order they are written. On its own, sequence always does exactly the same thing every time it runs.

Selection lets a program choose between different paths depending on a condition. It is built with if, elseif and else, or with a switch/case statement when you are checking one value against many possible options.

if score >= 50 then
    print("Pass")
elseif score >= 40 then
    print("Near miss")
else
    print("Try again")
endif

Iteration, also called looping, repeats a block of code so you do not have to write it out many times. There are two kinds. A count-controlled loop repeats a set number of times using a counter, which is ideal when you know exactly how many repeats you need. A condition-controlled loop keeps going until a condition is met, so the number of repeats can vary each time the program runs.

// count-controlled loop
for i = 1 to 5
    print("Hello")
next i

// condition-controlled loop
answer = ""
while answer != "yes"
    answer = input("Ready? ")
endwhile
Key Fact

Sequence, selection and iteration are the three constructs that control the flow of any program. Sequence runs steps in order, selection chooses between paths, and iteration repeats steps. Nearly every program is a mix of these three.

These building blocks are deliberately simple, yet they combine to make everything from a calculator to a search engine. When you plan a program, ask yourself three questions: what data do I need to store, what operators will change it, and which constructs will control when each step runs?
lessons.exam_tip_html: Watch out for two classic slips. First, keep = (store a value) separate from == (test whether two values are equal) — mixing them up is one of the most common mistakes. Second, know your operator words: DIV gives the whole-number part of a division and MOD gives the remainder, and examiners often ask you to work a quick MOD or DIV out by hand. When a question says ‘state’ or ‘give’, a short fact is enough; when it says ‘explain’, you must say why or how, usually with a brief example.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Variables hold values that can change; constants hold values that stay fixed. Assignment with = stores the value on the right into the variable on the left.
  • Operators act on data: arithmetic (including MOD, DIV and ^), comparison such as == and !=, and the Boolean operators AND, OR and NOT.
  • Sequence, selection and iteration are the three constructs that control the order in which a program’s instructions run.

lessons.title: Data Types & Structures
lessons.description: Integers, reals, Booleans, characters and strings, plus arrays and records for storing data.
lessons.content_html:
Computers do not really know the difference between a person’s age, a price in pounds, and the answer to a yes-or-no question — unless you tell them. A data type is the label a program attaches to a piece of data so the computer knows how to store it and what it is allowed to do with it. Choosing types well is one of the marks of a careful programmer.

The basic data types

A handful of types are used again and again. An integer is a whole number with nothing after a decimal point, so it suits counting things like lives, scores or the number of students in a class. A real number, sometimes called a float, has a decimal part, which makes it right for measurements and money, such as a height of 1.72 metres or a price of £19.99.

A Boolean can hold only one of two values, True or False. It is the natural choice for anything with a yes-or-no answer, such as whether a user is logged in or whether a game has been paused.

The last two deal with text. A character is a single symbol — one letter, digit, space or punctuation mark. A string is a sequence of characters joined together, so a name like “Ada Lovelace”, or even an empty piece of text, is a string. A string can contain digits, but if you store a phone number as a string you cannot do sums with it — it is text, not a number.

Key Fact

The quickest way to tell an integer from a real is the decimal point. Whole numbers with no decimal part are integers; numbers that need a decimal part, including most prices and measurements, are reals.

Casting: changing a value’s type

Casting means temporarily converting a value from one type to another. Functions such as int() and real() turn text into numbers, while str() turns a number back into text. The original value does not change type for good; casting simply gives you the value in the form you need at that moment.

Casting matters most when a program reads input. Whatever a user types at an input prompt arrives as a string, even when they type digits. To do arithmetic with it you must cast it first. So age = int(input("How old are you? ")) reads the text and converts it into an integer the program can add to or compare.

Imagine a program that asks for two numbers and adds them. If it reads them as strings and writes answer = first + second, then typing 2 and 3 gives “23”, because joining two strings sticks them end to end instead of adding them. Casting each input with int() first makes the program store whole numbers, so 2 and 3 correctly give 5. This is one of the most common bugs a new programmer meets.

Why the right data type matters

The type you choose decides three things. It decides which operations are allowed, because you can multiply two integers but not two Booleans. It affects how much memory is used, since a single character needs far less space than a long string. And it helps catch mistakes, because a program expecting an integer age can reject the text “banana” before it causes trouble later.

Key Fact

Choosing a suitable data type is not just tidy — it controls which operations you can perform, how much memory the data uses, and whether invalid data can be spotted early.

Data structures: arrays

Storing hundreds of values in separate variables would be a nightmare. An array solves this by holding many values of the same data type under a single name. Each value is reached by its index, a position number that starts at 0, so the first item is at index 0, the second at index 1, and so on. Arrays have a fixed length, meaning their size is set when they are created and does not change.

array colours[5]
colours[0] = "Blue"
colours[1] = "Pink"
print(colours[0])   // displays Blue

A one-dimensional (1D) array is a simple list. A two-dimensional (2D) array adds a second index so it behaves like a grid of rows and columns, which is ideal for a game board, a seating plan, or emulating the rows of a database table. You reach a cell with two numbers, one for the row and one for the column.

array board[3,3]
board[0,0] = "X"
board[1,2] = "O"
print(board[1,2])   // displays O

Suppose you need to store the marks of 30 students. Without an array you would need 30 separate variables and 30 lines just to add them up. With an array you can use a single loop that visits each index in turn, so the same few lines work whether there are 30 marks or 3000. This is why arrays and loops are so often used together.

Records

An array is perfect when every item is the same type, but real things often need several different pieces of information. A record groups related fields about one subject, and crucially those fields can be different data types. A single student record might hold a name as a string, an age as an integer, an average mark as a real, and whether fees are paid as a Boolean. You reach one field by its name, usually written with a dot.

student.name = "Ada"      // string
student.age = 15          // integer
student.average = 72.4    // real
student.feesPaid = true   // Boolean
print(student.name)       // displays Ada
Key Fact

The key difference is variety of type. An array holds many items of one single data type, whereas a record holds several fields about one thing and those fields can each be a different data type.

Put these ideas together and you can model almost any information. You might use a record to describe one student and an array to hold a whole class of those records — the right data type inside the right data structure. Whenever you plan a program, ask what kind of value each item is, and whether you are storing one of something or many.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Read the command word carefully. ‘State’ or ‘identify’ wants a short answer, such as naming a data type, while ‘explain’ wants a reason or a worked example.   • Casting temporarily converts a value from one type to another, which is essential because input always arrives as a string.
  • An array stores many values of the same type by index, while a record groups differently typed fields about one thing.

lessons.title: Advanced Programming Techniques
lessons.description: Structure programs with functions and procedures, use parameters, manage scope and handle files.
lessons.content_html:
Most real programs are far too large to write as one long list of instructions. If every line sat in a single block, the code would be hard to read, tricky to test and almost impossible to fix. The professional solution is to break a big problem into smaller, self-contained blocks of code that each do one job. Writing a program in this way is known as producing structured code.

A sub program is a named block of code that you can run whenever you need it, simply by writing its name. Because a sub program is written once but can be called many times, it saves you repeating the same instructions and keeps each part of the program short and focused. There are two kinds of sub program: procedures and functions.

Procedures and functions

A procedure is a sub program that carries out a task — such as printing a message or updating a score — but does not send any value back. You define it between the keywords procedure and endprocedure, then run it by writing its name followed by brackets.

procedure agePass()
    print("You are old enough to ride")
endprocedure

agePass()

A function also carries out a task, but it sends a single value back to the part of the program that called it. The value is passed back using the keyword return. Because a function produces a result, you normally store what it returns in a variable so you can use it later.

function squared(number)
    squared = number^2
    return squared
endfunction

newValue = squared(4)
Key Fact

A procedure performs a task but returns no value. A function performs a task and returns one value, which should be stored in a variable if you want to use it later.

Use a function whenever the sub program needs to work out or look up a value that the rest of the program will use — for example calculating a total, converting units or checking a password. The answer comes back through return.

Use a procedure when the sub program simply needs to do something and does not need to hand a value back — for example printing a menu, saving a file or clearing the screen. Choosing the right one makes your intentions clear to anyone reading the code.

Parameters and arguments

Sub programs become far more useful when you can feed data into them. A parameter is a variable listed in the sub program definition that receives an incoming value. An argument is the actual value you supply when you call the sub program. In the code below, width and height are parameters; when the sub program is called, the numbers 5 and 3 are the arguments.

procedure printArea(width, height)
    print(width * height)
endprocedure

printArea(5, 3)

Passing data through parameters means the same sub program can work on different values each time it is called, instead of being tied to one fixed set of numbers. This is exactly what makes sub programs reusable.

Variable scope: local and global

The scope of a variable describes which parts of a program are allowed to use it. A local variable is created inside a sub program and only exists while that sub program is running, so the rest of the program cannot see it. A global variable is declared in the main program and can be read or changed anywhere, including inside sub programs.

Key Fact

A local variable only exists inside the sub program where it is created and disappears when that sub program ends. A global variable can be accessed from anywhere in the program.

Because a local variable is sealed inside its own sub program, it cannot be changed by accident from somewhere else. This keeps sub programs independent, so you can change one without breaking another.

Global variables can be handy for data the whole program needs, but if many sub programs can all change the same global value, tracking down a bug becomes much harder. As a rule, keep variables local unless there is a clear reason to make them global.

Reading and writing files

A running program normally loses everything held in memory when it closes. To keep data permanently, a program can save it to a text file and read it back later — this is called file handling. There are four basic operations: open a file, read from it, write to it, and close it. When you open a file it must be stored in a variable so the program can work with it.

myFile = open("sample.txt")
print(myFile.readLine())
myFile.close()

The command readLine() returns the next line of the file each time it is used. To read a whole file you loop until you reach the end, which the endOfFile() command checks for you:

myFile = open("sample.txt")
while NOT myFile.endOfFile()
    print(myFile.readLine())
endwhile
myFile.close()

To store new data, writeLine() adds a line of text to the end of the file, and newFile() creates a brand new file ready to be opened. Always close a file with close() when you have finished, so that your changes are saved and the file is freed for other programs to use.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Watch the command word carefully. “State” or “identify” wants a quick fact, such as naming the keyword that ends a function, while “describe” and “explain” expect you to say how something works and why it is useful. A very common question asks for the difference between a function and a procedure — always mention the return value. If you are asked to write code, use clear names and neat indentation, because marks are given for readable, well-structured solutions as well as for correct logic.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Sub programs — functions and procedures — break a program into reusable, named blocks; only a function returns a value.
  • Parameters let you pass data into a sub program, and a variable’s scope decides whether it is local (inside one sub program) or global (usable everywhere).
  • File handling uses open, read, write and close so a program can store data permanently and read it back the next time it runs.

lessons.title: Defensive Design & Input Validation
lessons.description: How robust programs handle invalid input, confirm who users are and stay easy to maintain.
lessons.content_html:
Programs Have to Cope With Real People

When you test your own code, you type exactly what it expects. Real users are less predictable. They leave boxes blank, type letters where a number is needed, paste in a thousand characters, or tap buttons in the wrong order. Defensive design is the habit of writing a program that stays under control no matter what the user throws at it. A program that behaves like this is described as robust.

Getting this wrong is expensive. A program that is not robust can crash and lose the user’s work, store nonsense in a file, or open a security hole that lets an attacker in. Building defences in from the start is far cheaper than patching a broken program later, so professional programmers plan for bad input before they write a single line that trusts it.

Anticipating Misuse

Anticipating misuse means asking, before you write the code, “How might someone break this?” You then make sure each of those situations is handled instead of ignored. Some inputs cause a mistake by accident; others are deliberate attempts to make the program fail.

  • Leaving a required field completely empty.
  • Typing letters or symbols where a number is expected.
  • Entering an impossible value, such as an age of −5 or 300.
  • Giving a date that does not exist, like the 31st of February.
  • Pasting in an enormous amount of text to try to overload the program.

A well-designed program anticipates each case and responds gracefully. Instead of crashing, it shows a clear, polite message that tells the user what went wrong and how to fix it, then lets them try again. Guarding against a value that would break a calculation — such as dividing by zero — is another example of anticipating misuse.

Input Validation

Input validation is the most important defensive tool. It runs a series of checks on data the moment it is entered, and only lets the data through if it passes. Validation confirms that data is reasonable and allowable; it cannot prove the data is actually true. A validation check will happily accept the wrong-but-sensible age of 21, so validation reduces errors rather than removing them completely.

There are several standard checks, and a single field often uses more than one of them at once.

  • A presence check makes sure a required field has not been left empty.
  • A range check confirms a number falls between an acceptable lower and upper limit, such as a month between 1 and 12.
  • A type check confirms the data is the correct data type, for example a whole number rather than text.
  • A length check confirms the data has an acceptable number of characters, such as a password of at least eight.
  • A format check confirms the data follows a required pattern, such as an email address containing an “@” symbol.
Key Fact

The five common validation checks are presence, range, type, length and format. Presence rejects an empty box, range rejects a number that is too big or too small, type rejects the wrong data type, length rejects data with the wrong number of characters, and format rejects data that breaks the required pattern.

It is easy to assume that validated data must be correct, but that is not what validation promises. If a user is asked for their year of birth and types 1999 when they were really born in 2000, a range check sees a sensible four-digit year and lets it through. Validation only guarantees that data is possible and allowable, so a robust program still needs sensible defaults, clear instructions and helpful error messages to catch the mistakes that validation cannot see.

Authentication

Authentication protects a program by checking the identity of the person using it. The most common method is a username and password: the username says who you claim to be, and the password proves it because only the real account holder should know it. A program should compare the entered details against stored records and refuse access if they do not match.

Passwords are only useful if they are hard to guess. A strong password is a good length and mixes uppercase and lowercase letters, numbers and symbols, which makes it far harder for an attacker to work out. Many systems add extra layers, such as two-factor authentication — where a password is combined with a second check like a code sent to a phone — along with biometrics such as a fingerprint, or security questions. Each extra layer makes it harder for someone to pretend to be a genuine user.

Every extra character you add to a password multiplies the number of possible combinations an attacker would have to try. A short password made only of lowercase letters can be broken quickly by a computer testing millions of guesses, while a longer password that also uses capitals, digits and symbols has so many combinations that guessing becomes impractical. This is why systems often insist on a minimum length and a mixture of character types — a rule that is enforced using a length check and a format check.

Maintainability

Maintainability is a part of defensive design that is often forgotten. Programs are read, fixed and improved for years, often by a different programmer from the one who wrote them. Code that is tidy and clearly explained can be changed safely; code that is a tangled mess is where new bugs are introduced. Four simple habits make a program much easier to maintain.

First, use sub programs to break a large task into smaller named pieces. This avoids writing the same block of code twice, so if a mistake is found it only has to be fixed in one place. Second, follow sensible naming conventions so that a variable called totalPrice tells the reader exactly what it holds, unlike a vague name such as x.

Third, use consistent indentation so the shape of the code shows its structure — which lines sit inside a loop or a condition. Fourth, add comments to explain anything that is not obvious. A comment is written for the programmer, not the computer, so it never changes what the program does, but it can save hours of confusion later.

Key Fact

Four techniques improve maintainability: using sub programs to avoid repeated code, following clear naming conventions, indenting code to show its structure, and adding comments to explain how it works.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Watch the command word. “State” or “Identify” wants a short, named answer, while “Describe” and “Explain” expect you to say how or why as well. A very common mistake is to confuse validation with authentication: validation checks that data is sensible, while authentication checks that a user is genuine — keep the two separate. When you name a validation check, always back it up with a concrete example of an input it would reject, because the example is usually where the marks are.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Defensive design builds a robust program that anticipates misuse and stays under control when users enter unexpected input.
  • Input validation uses presence, range, type, length and format checks to keep out unsuitable data, and authentication confirms a user really is who they claim to be.
  • Sub programs, clear naming conventions, indentation and comments make a program easier and safer to maintain in the future.

lessons.title: Testing & Debugging
lessons.description: How to test programs with the right data and track down bugs before users find them.
lessons.content_html:
However carefully a program is written, mistakes creep in. A bug is any error in the code that stops the program working the way it should. Testing is the process of running a program with carefully chosen data to reveal these bugs so they can be fixed before real users ever see them.

The purpose of testing is to check that a program meets its requirements, produces the correct output for every likely input, and keeps working without crashing. Good testing also proves that a program is robust — it copes sensibly with unexpected or silly data instead of falling over. It is worth remembering that testing can reveal that bugs exist, but it can never prove that a program is completely free of them.

Key Fact

Testing checks that a program meets its requirements, gives correct outputs for all likely inputs, and is robust enough to handle unexpected data. It can show that bugs are present but never prove that none remain.

Testing as you go, and testing at the end

Programmers test in two different ways at two different stages. Iterative testing happens all the way through development. Each time a small section or module is written, the programmer runs it, checks it works, fixes anything wrong, then moves on. Because problems are caught early and in small pieces of code, they are far easier to locate and put right.

Final testing, also called terminal testing, is carried out once the whole program is finished. Now that the separate modules are joined together, the aim is to check that the complete system works as one and meets every requirement. Some faults only appear when parts of a program interact, so this final stage catches problems that module-by-module testing can miss.

If you write two hundred lines of code and only test at the very end, a single wrong result could be hiding anywhere. By testing each module as you build it, you already know the earlier parts work, so any new bug is almost certainly in the code you just added. This is why iterative testing saves so much time compared with leaving everything to the end.

Two kinds of error: syntax and logic

A syntax error breaks the grammatical rules of the programming language. A missing bracket, a misspelled keyword, or a colon left off the end of a line all count. Because the translator cannot understand the code, a syntax error stops the program from being translated or run at all. The good news is that these errors are usually flagged straight away, often with the line number where the problem was found.

A logic error is sneakier. The code obeys all the grammar rules, so it runs perfectly happily — but it produces the wrong output. Using a plus sign where you meant a minus, or checking ‘greater than’ when you meant ‘greater than or equal to’, will not stop the program, yet the answers will be wrong. Because nothing crashes, logic errors are the hardest to spot.

Key Fact

A syntax error breaks the rules of the language and stops the program running or being translated. A logic error lets the program run but produces unexpected, incorrect output.

Suppose a program should add VAT to a price. If you write prnt(total) instead of print(total), the translator does not recognise the command and reports a syntax error before the program even runs. But if you accidentally multiply the price by 1.02 when VAT is 20 per cent, the program runs fine and simply gives the wrong total — that is a logic error. Same program, two very different kinds of mistake.

Choosing good test data

Testing only with sensible, everyday values is not enough. A thorough test tries the edges and the rubbish too. There are four types of test data you should be able to choose for any scenario. Imagine a program that accepts a school year group, where only whole numbers from 7 to 11 are allowed.

  • Normal test data is data that should be accepted without causing errors — sensible, typical values. Example: 9.
  • Boundary test data is data of the correct type that sits right on the very edge of what is allowed. You test both sides of each edge: 7 and 11 should be accepted, while 6 and 12 should be rejected.
  • Invalid test data is data of the correct type that should still be rejected. Example: 15 — it is a whole number, but it lies outside the allowed range.
  • Erroneous test data is data of the wrong type altogether that should be rejected. Example: the word ‘nine’, because text cannot be a year-group number.
Key Fact

The difference between invalid and erroneous data is the data type. Invalid data is the correct type but out of range and should be rejected. Erroneous data is the wrong type entirely and should also be rejected.

Recording tests: the test plan

Professionals do not test at random and hope for the best. They write a test plan — a table listing each test, the data used, the type of test, the result expected, and the result that actually happened. If the actual result matches the expected result, the test passes; if not, a bug has been found and needs fixing. A strong test plan includes normal, boundary, invalid and erroneous data so that nothing is left unchecked.

Test dataTypeExpected result
9NormalAccepted

Debugging: finding and fixing bugs

When a test fails, the next job is debugging — tracking down the exact cause of a bug and correcting it. Syntax errors are usually easy: the translator points to the line and often describes what is wrong. Logic errors take far more detective work, because the program runs without complaint and gives no clue where it went astray.

The most reliable way to hunt a logic error is to follow the code by hand, one line at a time, writing down how each variable changes. This is called a dry run, and the table you fill in is a trace table. Comparing the values the variables actually hold against the values they should hold reveals exactly where the program goes wrong. Adding temporary lines that print a variable’s value at key points does a similar job while the program is running.

Faced with a failing program, work methodically. First, read any error message carefully — it often names the line and the problem. Next, narrow down where the fault lies by checking the output of each module in turn. Then trace the suspect section by hand to see where a variable takes the wrong value. Finally, make one change at a time and re-test, so you always know which fix actually worked. Changing lots of things at once usually just creates new bugs.

Refining the solution

Testing and debugging feed into refining — improving the program once faults have been found. Refining might mean correcting an error, but it can also mean tightening up the logic, adding a check for input the programmer had not thought of, or rewriting a clumsy section so it runs faster or reads more clearly. Development is a cycle: write, test, debug, refine, then test again until the program is genuinely reliable.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Questions on this topic love the word ‘identify’ or ‘give’ — if you are given a scenario with a valid range, be ready to name matching normal, boundary, invalid and erroneous data. The mark most often lost is confusing invalid with erroneous: remember invalid data is the right type but out of range, while erroneous data is the wrong type completely. When a ‘describe’ or ‘explain’ question mentions a program that runs but gives the wrong answer, that is your cue to write about logic errors and how a trace table or dry run helps you find them.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Iterative testing checks modules as they are written; final (terminal) testing checks the whole finished program works together.
  • Syntax errors break the language rules and stop the program running; logic errors let it run but produce the wrong output.
  • Test with normal, boundary, invalid and erroneous data, record it in a test plan, then debug and refine until the program is reliable.

lessons.title: Boolean Logic & Truth Tables
lessons.description: Meet the AND, OR and NOT gates, build truth tables, and combine gates to solve logic problems.
lessons.content_html:
Deep inside every computer, all data — numbers, letters, images and sounds — is stored as Boolean values: long streams of 1s and 0s. Boolean logic is the set of rules a computer follows to make decisions using just these two values, where 1 means true (or ‘on’) and 0 means false (or ‘off’). Almost every action a machine takes, from unlocking a phone to deciding whether a game character can jump, comes down to combinations of trues and falses.

Each of those decisions is built from tiny electronic components called logic gates. A logic gate takes one or more binary inputs and produces a single binary output, always following the same fixed rule. Millions of these gates sit inside the arithmetic logic unit, the part of the processor that carries out calculations and logical comparisons. The whole system is named after George Boole, a 19th-century English mathematician who first set out this kind of algebra long before computers existed.

Key Fact

There are three fundamental logic gates you must know: AND, OR and NOT. Any circuit, however large or complex, can be built by combining just these three.

The AND gate

An AND gate has two inputs and one output. Its output is 1 only when both inputs are 1; if either input is 0, the output is 0. A helpful picture is two switches wired one after the other (in series) — the current can only flow when both switches are closed at the same time. To record how any gate behaves we use a truth table, which lists every possible combination of inputs and shows the output for each.

Input AInput BOutput Q
000
010
100
111

Notice there is only a single 1 in the output column — on the bottom row, the one row where both inputs are 1.

The OR gate

An OR gate also has two inputs and one output, but its output is 1 when at least one input is 1. The only way to get an output of 0 is for both inputs to be 0 together. Picture two switches wired side by side (in parallel): the current flows if either one of them is closed.

Input AInput BOutput Q
000
011
101
111

This time there is only a single 0 in the output column, on the top row where both inputs are 0. Everywhere else the output is 1.

The NOT gate

A NOT gate works differently: it has just one input and one output. It simply reverses, or inverts, whatever it is given, so an input of 0 becomes 1 and an input of 1 becomes 0. Because it flips the signal, a NOT gate is often called an inverter. Its truth table is the shortest of the three.

Input AOutput Q
01
10

Each gate is drawn with its own distinctive shape inside a logic diagram. The AND gate is drawn with a flat back and a rounded front, so it looks like a capital letter D. The OR gate has a curved back and narrows to a point at the output, giving it a shield or spaceship shape.

The NOT gate is drawn as a small triangle pointing towards its output, with a tiny circle (called a bubble) on the very tip. That bubble is the giveaway that the signal is being inverted — if you ever see it, you know the gate flips its input.

Key Fact

The number of rows a truth table needs depends on how many inputs the circuit has. For a circuit with \(n\) inputs, the table needs \(2^n\) rows — so 1 input needs 2 rows, 2 inputs need 4 rows, and 3 inputs need 8 rows.

Combining logic gates

Real circuits usually join several gates together, and this is exactly the same idea as using AND, OR and NOT inside the conditions of a program. To read a combined circuit, work out the output of each gate one step at a time, following the signals from the inputs through to the final output. Writing the circuit as a Boolean expression first makes this much easier to track.

Take a circuit written as Q = (A AND B) OR C. To build its full truth table, first list all \(2^3 = 8\) possible combinations of A, B and C. Next add a helper column that works out A AND B for each row. Finally work out Q by applying OR to that helper column and to C. The brackets tell you to deal with the AND gate before the OR gate.

ABCA AND BQ
00000
00101
01000
01101
10000
10101
11011
11111

A Boolean expression is a shorthand way of describing a circuit without drawing it. You can spell the operators out in words — A AND B — or use symbols, where a dot stands for AND, a plus sign stands for OR, and a bar written over a letter stands for NOT. Brackets show which operation to work out first, exactly as they do in ordinary maths.

The real skill is being able to move freely between four different ways of describing the same logic: a written description in plain English, a Boolean expression, a logic diagram of gates, and a completed truth table. Each one contains exactly the same information, just presented differently.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When a question asks you to complete a truth table, always list the input combinations in a steady binary counting order (00, 01, 10, 11) so you never miss a row, and add a helper column for each intermediate gate before working out the final output. Watch the command words carefully: ‘complete’ means fill in a table, ‘draw’ means produce a labelled logic diagram using the correct gate symbols, and ‘explain’ means give the reason behind an output, not just the answer.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • An AND gate outputs 1 only when both inputs are 1; an OR gate outputs 1 when at least one input is 1; a NOT gate reverses its single input.
  • A truth table lists every input combination and its output, and needs \(2^n\) rows for a circuit with \(n\) inputs.
  • Combined circuits are solved one gate at a time, and the same logic can be shown as words, a Boolean expression, a logic diagram or a truth table.

lessons.title: Programming Languages & IDEs
lessons.description: How high-level and low-level languages, compilers, interpreters and IDEs turn code into software.
lessons.content_html:
Computers ultimately understand only one thing: patterns of binary 1s and 0s. Yet almost nobody writes programs directly in binary — it would be painfully slow and terribly easy to get wrong. Instead, programmers pick a language that suits the job and rely on other software to turn their code into something the processor can actually run. This lesson looks at the different levels of programming language, the translators that convert your code, and the toolkit that makes writing software far quicker.

High-level and low-level languages

Programming languages sit on a scale, depending on how close they are to human language or to the raw instructions of the processor. A high-level language such as Python, Java or C++ is written using English-like keywords such as ‘if’, ‘print’ and ‘while’. A single line of high-level code usually stands in for many processor instructions. This makes high-level code easier to read, write and debug, and it is portable — the same program can run on different types of computer once it has been translated. Its one catch is that it must always be translated before the processor can understand it.

A low-level language is much closer to the hardware. The lowest level is machine code — pure binary that the processor runs directly, with no translation needed. Assembly language is also low-level, replacing binary with short memory-joggers called mnemonics. Low-level code is hard for people to read and write, and it is machine-specific, so it only works on one type of processor. In return it runs very fast, uses little memory and gives the programmer precise control over the hardware, which is why it is used for tasks like device drivers and other software that must squeeze the most out of the machine.

Key Fact

High-level languages use English-like keywords, are easy to read and debug, and are portable across different machines. Low-level languages are close to the hardware: harder to write and machine-specific, but faster and more memory-efficient.

Because one high-level statement replaces many machine-code instructions, programmers can build software much faster and with fewer mistakes. A program written once in a high-level language can also be translated to run on many different computers, whereas low-level code usually has to be rewritten for each new type of processor. For most everyday software, that productivity and portability easily outweigh the small loss of speed.

Translators: compilers and interpreters

Because a processor can only run machine code, any program written in a high-level language has to be converted first. A translator is a program that turns source code — the code a programmer writes — into machine code. The two translators you need to know are the compiler and the interpreter. They do the same job in very different ways.

A compiler translates the entire program in one go, before it is run. It produces a separate executable file of machine code that can then be run on its own, without the source code or the compiler being present. Compiling a large program can take a while, but the finished executable then runs quickly. A compiler checks the whole program and produces an error report at the end, listing the mistakes together rather than stopping at the first one.

An interpreter translates and runs the program one statement at a time. It does not create an executable file, so the interpreter and the source code are both needed every time the program runs. Because it translates as it goes, an interpreted program runs more slowly. However, the interpreter stops at the very first error it meets and reports it straight away, which makes mistakes much easier to find and fix while a program is still being developed.

Key Fact

A compiler translates the whole program at once into a fast, standalone executable, but reports all its errors together at the end. An interpreter translates line by line, runs more slowly and needs the source code each time, but stops at the first error, making debugging easier.

A compiler is a good choice for finished software you want to share. The executable runs fast, works without the original source code, and keeps that source code hidden from users. The drawbacks are that you must recompile the whole program after every change, and the executable only runs on the type of processor it was built for.

An interpreter suits writing and testing programs. Errors are caught one at a time, and the same source code will run on any device that has the right interpreter, which makes it very portable. The trade-offs are slower running speed and the fact that the source code must be handed over to anyone who wants to run the program.

Integrated Development Environments

Writing, running and fixing code in separate programs would be slow, so programmers use an Integrated Development Environment, or IDE — a single application that brings all the tools they need into one place. Popular examples include IDLE for Python, PyCharm and Visual Studio. An IDE usually provides four kinds of tool.

  • Editor — where you type your code. Helpful features such as colour-coded keywords (syntax highlighting), automatic indentation, auto-complete and line numbering make code faster to write and easier to read.
  • Error diagnostics — tools that help track down mistakes. A breakpoint pauses the program at a chosen line, and the programmer can then step through the code line by line and watch how the values stored in variables change, pinpointing where a fault happens.
  • Run-time environment — a run-time environment lets the programmer run the program from inside the IDE and see its output straight away.
  • Translator — a built-in compiler or interpreter that converts the code into machine code so it can actually run.

Because all of these tools sit in one window, an IDE speeds up the whole write, run and debug cycle. That is why almost all software today is created using one.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Watch the command word carefully. ‘State’ or ‘Give’ wants a quick fact with no explanation, while ‘Describe’ and especially ‘Explain’ expect you to say how or why. A very common question asks you to compare a compiler and an interpreter — make sure each point is a genuine contrast (for example, ‘a compiler translates all the code at once, whereas an interpreter translates one line at a time’) rather than two facts that never mention each other. When a question is about an IDE, name a specific tool and then say exactly how it helps the programmer, not just what it is.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • High-level languages are written in English-like keywords and are portable and easy to debug; low-level languages sit close to the hardware and are fast but machine-specific.
  • A compiler translates the whole program at once into a standalone executable, while an interpreter translates and runs it line by line, stopping at the first error.
  • An IDE combines an editor, error-diagnostic tools, a run-time environment and a translator so that code can be written, run and fixed in one place.

practice_questions.marks: A correct response identifies a defining feature, such as: it uses English-like keywords; it is easy for people to read and write; one statement stands in for many machine instructions; it is portable across different machines; or it must be translated before it can run. A single clear characteristic gains the mark.

practice_questions.text: Describe one difference between a high-level language and a low-level language.
practice_questions.marks: Secure: a clear contrast made on the same measure — for example, that a high-level language uses English-like keywords and is portable across machines, whereas a low-level language is written closer to the hardware, is machine-specific and is harder for people to read. Developing: two unconnected facts about each language, or a difference only hinted at. Emerging: one vague or inaccurate point.

practice_questions.text: Explain why a program written in a high-level language needs a translator before it can run.
practice_questions.marks: Secure: explains that the processor can only execute machine code (binary), so a translator is needed to convert the high-level source code into machine code that the computer can run. One mark for identifying that the processor only understands machine code, a second for the point that the translator converts the code so it can be executed. Developing: states that code must be translated without saying why.

practice_questions.text: Explain two differences between how a compiler and an interpreter work.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: two clear, correctly contrasted differences, each developed — for example, a compiler translates the whole program before it runs while an interpreter translates and runs one statement at a time; and a compiler produces a standalone executable while an interpreter needs the source code and interpreter present every time. Secure: two valid differences with some explanation. Developing: one difference explained, or two only stated. Emerging: a relevant point about either translator with limited accuracy.

practice_questions.text: Describe three tools that an Integrated Development Environment provides to help a programmer, and how each one helps.
practice_questions.marks: Secure: three distinct IDE tools, each with a brief note of how it helps — for example an editor (typing code with syntax highlighting and auto-indentation), error-diagnostic or debugging tools (breakpoints to pause and inspect the program), a run-time environment (running the program and viewing its output), or a built-in translator (converting the code so it can run). One mark per correctly described tool. Naming a tool without saying how it helps is developing.

practice_questions.text: A developer is writing and testing a new program and must decide whether to use a compiler or an interpreter. Discuss the benefits and drawbacks of each, and recommend which she should use while she is still developing the program.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: a balanced discussion covering benefits and drawbacks of both translators, applied to the scenario, leading to a justified recommendation — for example, an interpreter during development because it stops at the first error and makes debugging quick, despite its slower running speed. Secure: clear benefits and drawbacks of both translators with a supported recommendation. Developing: some relevant points, mostly one-sided, with a limited or unsupported judgement. Emerging: a few basic points about either translator with no real comparison or conclusion.

glossary_terms.definition: A programming language that uses English-like keywords, is easy for people to read and write, and must be translated before a computer can run it.
A programming language that is close to the hardware, such as machine code, which is fast and machine-specific but hard for people to read and write.
Binary instructions that a processor can execute directly, without any translation.
A program that converts source code into machine code so that the processor can run it.
The code a programmer writes in a programming language, before it is translated into machine code.
A translator that converts the whole program into machine code in one go, producing an executable file that can be run on its own.
A ready-to-run file of machine code produced by a compiler, which runs without needing the source code or the translator.
A translator that converts and runs a program one statement at a time, needing the source code and interpreter present every time.
A single application that brings together the tools a programmer needs to write, run and debug programs.
A marker that pauses a running program at a chosen line so the programmer can inspect it.
The part of an IDE that lets a programmer run a program and see its output without needing separate software.
